method: Title taken from the h1 element (the clean comma-structured product name); the <title> element was used only as a fallback, with its " - Category - SKU|MPN - Grainger Industrial Supply" tail stripped. The title is split on its delimiter. Segment 1 is the ITEM. Every later segment is resolved against THAT RECORD'S OWN attribute values: exact value match, value-then-label prefix match, inch-normalised numeric match, or short-prefix value abbreviation. The label is whatever text remains after the value. NO abbreviation was resolved by guessing its meaning -- every mapping in abbreviation_lexicon is backed by a value match in the same record, and the support count is given. Segments no attribute corroborates are reported verbatim as unresolved, with their record's full attribute set as context so a human can extend the lexicon.
grammar: TITLE := ITEM (DELIM SEGMENT)*   ;   SEGMENT := VALUE LABEL? -- VALUE PRECEDES its LABEL. VALUE is textual or dimensional. LABEL may be omitted entirely (bare value), abbreviated, or character-truncated when the title hits its length cap.

title_token_vs_assumed_attribute.method: For every record carrying a milling diameter, each title segment containing a dimension token was normalised to inches and compared against that record's own Milling Dia. Segments were also classified by whether they carry a LABEL at all. The hazard the demo reproduces is a dimension in the title that a shopper would read as the cutting diameter but is not -- which happens two ways: an UNLABELLED token that is not the milling diameter, and a token labelled with a secondary dimension (neck, reach, shank, corner radius) that a scanning shopper still reads as the headline size.
